name: health-economics
description: Rust implementations of 91 health-economics metrics and their software engineering analogues.
license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0-only OR GPL-3.0-only

conventions.numeric_type: f64 everywhere, except 3 modules using rusty_money::Money<'static, iso::Currency> for exact-decimal currency arithmetic
conventions.fallible_return: Option<f64> when a denominator can be zero (None, never NaN/inf); Result<_, MoneyError> for the 3 Money-based modules
conventions.panics: no public function panics; float sorts use f64::total_cmp

modules.name: quality_adjusted_life_year
modules.title: Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY)
modules.summary: A QALY is one year of life lived in perfect health. It combines *how long* people live with *how well* they live, so that a year in poor health counts as less than one QALY — making utterly different health interventions comparable on a single scale.

functions.name: qaly_loss_from_delay
functions.signature: qaly_loss_from_delay(delay_years: f64, utility_waiting: f64, utility_treated: f64) -> f64

modules.name: eq_5d
modules.title: EQ-5D
modules.summary: EQ-5D is the `EuroQol` group's standardized questionnaire for measuring health-related quality of life. It is the instrument that produces the utility weights inside most QALY calculations — NICE's reference case names it the preferred measure for adults.

functions.name: qaly_gain
functions.signature: qaly_gain(utility_before: f64, utility_after: f64, duration_years: f64) -> f64

modules.name: disability_adjusted_life_year
modules.title: Disability-Adjusted Life Year (DALY)
modules.summary: A DALY is one lost year of healthy life — the burden-side mirror of the QALY. Where QALYs count health *gained*, DALYs count health *lost* to disease; interventions are valued by DALYs **averted**.

functions.name: who_choice_band
functions.formula: `HighlyCostEffective` if `cost_per_daly_averted < gdp_per_capita`; else `CostEffective` if `cost_per_daly_averted <= 3.0 * gdp_per_capita`; else `NotCostEffective`

modules.name: life_years_gained
modules.title: Life-Years Gained (LYG)
modules.summary: Life-years gained is the additional survival attributable to an intervention, with no quality adjustment: the area between the survival curves with and without it.

functions.name: area_between_survival_curves
functions.formula: trapezoidal-rule integral of the gap curve `g(t) = survival_new(t) − survival_comparator(t)` over `times`: `Σ_i dt_i × (g(t_{i-1}) + g(t_i)) / 2`, restricted to the sampled horizon (no extrapolation beyond the last time point). `times` must be increasing.

modules.name: health_adjusted_life_expectancy
modules.title: Health-Adjusted Life Expectancy (HALE)
modules.summary: HALE is a population-level summary: the number of years a person can expect to live *in full health*, discounting years spent in illness or disability. Global HALE at birth was about 61.9 years against a life expectancy of 73.3 (WHO, 2019 data) — humanity lives its last decade, on average, in less-than-full health.

functions.name: proportion_in_full_health
functions.formula: `1 − Σ (prevalence × disability_weight)` over `conditions`. Assumes independent, additive burdens; with high prevalences or many comorbid conditions the sum can exceed 1 and the result go negative.

functions.name: sullivan_hale
functions.formula: `Σ (person_years[i] × full_health_proportion[i]) / survivors_at_x` (Sullivan method); with every proportion at 1.0 this reduces to ordinary life expectancy `Σ L_a / l_x`.

modules.name: patient_reported_outcomes
modules.title: Patient-Reported Outcomes (PROMs, PREMs, MCID)
modules.summary: PROMs are standardized instruments where patients report their own health status (symptoms, function, quality of life); PREMs capture the care *experience*. The **MCID** — minimal clinically important difference — is the smallest score change patients actually perceive as beneficial: the bar any claimed improvement must clear.

functions.name: instrument_sum_score
functions.formula: `Σ item_responses` (e.g. PHQ-9 = sum of 9 items each 0–3)

functions.name: number_needed_to_treat
functions.returns_none_when: `absolute_risk_reduction == 0.0` (the arms do not differ, so NNT is undefined/infinite); a negative ARR yields a negative value (a number needed to harm).

modules.name: number_needed_to_treat
modules.title: Number Needed to Treat (NNT)
modules.summary: NNT is the number of patients who must receive an intervention for **one** additional patient to benefit, over a stated time frame. It converts percentage risk reductions — which mislead — into effort-per-benefit units that anyone can reason about.

modules.name: work_productivity_and_activity_impairment
modules.title: Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI)
modules.summary: WPAI is a validated self-report questionnaire (Reilly, Zbrozek, Dasbach, 1993) measuring how much a health problem affects paid work and daily activities, usually over the past 7 days. It splits the loss into *absenteeism* — work time literally missed — and *presenteeism* — reduced productivity while physically at work — and the second is usually the larger, more hidden cost component.

modules.name: time_trade_off_utility
modules.title: Time Trade-Off (TTO) Utility Elicitation
modules.summary: TTO (Torrance, 1976) is a standard method for eliciting a health-state utility value directly from a respondent, rather than inventing one. For a state considered *better than death*, the respondent is asked how many years `X` in full health they would consider equivalent to `T` years in the impaired state (`X < T`); utility is `X / T`.

modules.name: cost_effectiveness_analysis
modules.title: Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA)
modules.summary: CEA compares the costs of alternative interventions against a single outcome measured in **natural units** — life-years, cases detected, admissions avoided, mmHg of blood pressure reduced. Its output is a cost per unit of outcome.

functions.name: icer
functions.signature: icer(cost_a: f64, effect_a: f64, cost_b: f64, effect_b: f64) -> Option<f64>

functions.name: incremental_icers
functions.formula: for each adjacent pair `(pair[0], pair[1])` in `options_sorted_by_effect.windows(2)`, `icer(pair[1].cost, pair[1].effect, pair[0].cost, pair[0].effect)`
functions.example: for the three-option worked example (pulse checks £150k/300, pharmacy £400k/520, wearable £900k/610), `incremental_icers(&options)[0].unwrap() ≈ 1_136.0` and `[1].unwrap() ≈ 5_556.0`

modules.name: cost_utility_analysis
modules.title: Cost-Utility Analysis (CUA)
modules.summary: CUA is cost-effectiveness analysis with a **generic, preference-weighted outcome** — almost always the QALY (or DALY averted). Because the outcome unit is universal, CUA can compare interventions across completely different diseases.

modules.name: cost_benefit_analysis
modules.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA)
modules.summary: CBA values both costs *and* outcomes in money. It is the only analysis type that can answer "is this worth doing at all?" — not merely "which option is best?" — because monetized benefits can be compared directly against costs.

functions.name: present_value
functions.formula: `Σ_t flows_by_year[t] / (1 + rate)^t`, where index `t` is the year (index 0 = year 0, undiscounted)

modules.name: cost_minimization_analysis
modules.title: Cost-Minimization Analysis (CMA)
modules.summary: CMA compares only costs, and picks the cheapest option — legitimate *only* when the outcomes of the alternatives have been demonstrated to be equivalent.

functions.name: outcomes_equivalent
functions.signature: outcomes_equivalent(effect_a: f64, effect_b: f64, margin: f64) -> bool

functions.name: cost_minimization
functions.signature: cost_minimization(cost_a: f64, cost_b: f64, equivalence_evidenced: bool) -> Option<Selection>
functions.formula: if `equivalence_evidenced`, `Some(if cost_b < cost_a { OptionB } else { OptionA })`
functions.returns_none_when: `equivalence_evidenced == false` (CMA is invalid without evidenced equivalence — use CEA/CUA instead).

modules.name: cost_consequence_analysis
modules.title: Cost-Consequence Analysis (CCA)
modules.summary: CCA presents costs alongside a **disaggregated table of all outcomes** — clinical, operational, experiential — without collapsing them into a single ratio or score. The decision-maker weighs the trade-offs explicitly.

modules.name: budget_impact_analysis
modules.title: Budget Impact Analysis (BIA)
modules.summary: BIA estimates what adopting an intervention does to a specific payer's **budget** over the next 1–5 years. It answers *affordability*; cost-effectiveness answers *value*.

functions.name: net_cost_per_patient
functions.signature: net_cost_per_patient(intervention_cost: f64, displaced_care_cost: f64, induced_care_cost: f64) -> f64

modules.name: social_return_on_investment
modules.title: Social Return on Investment (SROI)
modules.summary: SROI extends ROI to outcomes that markets don't price — wellbeing, social connection, carer relief, environmental impact — by monetizing them with financial proxies, for *all* stakeholders affected.

functions.name: total_outcome_value
functions.example: for the loneliness outcome (value £1,620,000) and a GP outcome (quantity 1,800.0, proxy 42.0, attribution 1.0, no deadweight/ displacement, value £75,600), `total_outcome_value(&[loneliness, gp]) == 1_695_600.0`

functions.name: value_after_drop_off
functions.signature: value_after_drop_off(initial_value: f64, drop_off_rate: f64, years: u32) -> f64
functions.formula: `initial_value * (1 - drop_off_rate)^years` (geometric decay; year 0 returns the value unchanged)

modules.name: health_technology_assessment
modules.title: Health Technology Assessment (HTA)
modules.summary: HTA is the formal, institutionalized process by which health systems decide whether a technology — drug, device, or software — is worth paying for. It combines clinical-effectiveness evidence with economic evaluation under a published, mandatory methodology.

functions.name: meets_threshold
functions.formula: `icer_value < threshold` (strict comparison; an ICER exactly equal to the threshold does not clear it)

functions.name: probability_cost_effective
functions.formula: fraction of `psa_draws` (each a `(ΔC, ΔE)` pair) for which `ΔE × lambda − ΔC > 0` (net monetary benefit strictly positive; equivalent to `ICER < lambda` but avoids division so `ΔE` near zero cannot blow up the statistic)
functions.example: 71 draws of `(450.0, 0.03)` (NMB > 0) and 29 draws of `(450.0, 0.01)` (NMB < 0) at `lambda = 20_000.0` → `probability_cost_effective(&draws, 20_000.0) == Some(0.71)`

functions.name: recommend_routine_commissioning
functions.example: conformant checklist, `icer_value = 15_000.0`, `threshold = 20_000.0` → `true`; a strawman-comparator checklist with `icer_value = 9_000.0` → `false`

modules.name: human_capital_and_friction_cost
modules.title: Human Capital Approach vs Friction Cost Method
modules.summary: These are the two competing methods for valuing lost productivity — from illness, disability, or death — in cost-of-illness and cost-benefit studies. The Human Capital Approach (HCA) values all lost output for the full duration of absence at the wage rate; the Friction Cost Method (FCM) values it only for the shorter period an employer actually needs to restore production.

functions.name: friction_cost
functions.signature: friction_cost(daily_wage: f64, days_lost: f64, friction_period_days: f64) -> f64

modules.name: markov_cohort_simulation
modules.title: Markov Cohort Simulation
modules.summary: The standard HTA modelling technique for interventions whose effects unfold over multiple time periods (cycles): a hypothetical cohort starts entirely in one health state, and each cycle a fixed set of transition probabilities move fractions of the cohort between states. Costs and QALYs accrue each cycle in proportion to how much of the cohort occupies each state, and are discounted back to present value.

functions.name: advance_cohort
functions.returns_none_when: `transition_matrix.len() != state.len()`, or any row's length `!= state.len()` (malformed shape — never indexes out of bounds).

functions.name: simulate_cohort
functions.signature: simulate_cohort(initial_distribution: &[f64], transition_matrix: &[Vec<f64>], cost_per_cycle: &[f64], utility: &[f64], cycle_length_years: f64, cycles: usize, discount_rate: f64) -> Option<(f64, f64)>
functions.formula: runs `cycle_cost`/`cycle_qalys` on each cycle's state, discounts each cycle's values by `1 / (1 + discount_rate)^t`, sums both series, and advances the cohort via `advance_cohort` between cycles. Returns `(total_discounted_cost, total_discounted_qalys)`.
functions.returns_none_when: `initial_distribution`, `transition_matrix`, `cost_per_cycle`, or `utility` have mismatched shapes (propagated from the three functions above).
functions.example: a 2-state Well/Dead model (`initial_distribution = [1.0, 0.0]`, `transition_matrix = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0]]`, `cost_per_cycle = [1_000.0, 0.0]`, `utility = [0.8, 0.0]`, `cycle_length_years = 1.0`, `cycles = 3`, `discount_rate = 0.035`) gives `total_discounted_cost ≈ 2_625.708_884_688_091` and `total_discounted_qalys ≈ 2.100_567_107_750_473_3` (verified by running the code, not hand-derived).

modules.name: incremental_cost_effectiveness_ratio
modules.title: Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER)
modules.summary: The ICER is the extra cost per extra unit of health effect when you choose one option over the next-best alternative. It is the headline number of health technology assessment.

functions.name: classify_quadrant
functions.formula: Formula/rules (checked in this order): `delta_effect == 0.0` → `OnAxis`; else `delta_cost <= 0.0 && delta_effect > 0.0` → `Dominant`; else `delta_cost > 0.0 && delta_effect > 0.0` → `TradeOff`; else `delta_cost > 0.0` (with `delta_effect < 0.0`) → `Dominated`; else (`delta_cost <= 0.0 && delta_effect < 0.0`) → `SavingsForLoss`.

functions.name: adopt_at_threshold
functions.formula: `icer_value < lambda` (strict comparison); only meaningful in the `TradeOff` quadrant — dominant and dominated options are decided by quadrant alone.

modules.name: net_monetary_benefit
modules.title: Net Monetary Benefit (NMB)
modules.summary: NMB converts a cost-effectiveness result into a single money value: health gain priced at the willingness-to-pay threshold, minus cost. Its twin, Net Health Benefit (NHB), expresses the same rule in health units.

functions.name: net_monetary_benefit
functions.signature: net_monetary_benefit(delta_effect: f64, delta_cost: f64, lambda: f64) -> f64

functions.name: net_health_benefit
functions.signature: net_health_benefit(delta_effect: f64, delta_cost: f64, lambda: f64) -> Option<f64>

functions.name: adopt
functions.formula: `nmb > 0.0` (decision rule: adopt if NMB is strictly positive)

functions.name: best_option_index
functions.formula: computes `net_monetary_benefit` for each option at `lambda` and returns the index of the highest; ties keep the earliest option (a later option must strictly exceed the incumbent to win).

modules.name: willingness_to_pay_thresholds
modules.title: Willingness-to-Pay Thresholds
modules.summary: A willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold is the maximum a decision-maker will pay per unit of health gain — the line λ that turns an ICER (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio) into an adopt/reject decision.

functions.name: net_monetary_benefit
functions.signature: net_monetary_benefit(threshold: f64, incremental_effect: f64, incremental_cost: f64) -> f64

functions.name: adopt_by_icer
functions.signature: adopt_by_icer(incremental_cost: f64, incremental_effect: f64, threshold: f64) -> Option<bool>
functions.returns_none_when: `incremental_effect == 0.0` (no ICER exists; use `adopt_by_nmb` instead, which is defined even at `incremental_effect == 0.0`)

functions.name: adopt_by_nmb
functions.signature: adopt_by_nmb(threshold: f64, incremental_effect: f64, incremental_cost: f64) -> bool

functions.name: max_defensible_price
functions.signature: max_defensible_price(threshold: f64, qalys_gained: f64, cost_offsets: f64) -> f64

modules.name: dominance_and_efficiency_frontier
modules.title: Dominance and the Efficiency Frontier
modules.summary: An option is **dominated** if another option costs less *and* delivers more. The **efficiency frontier** is what remains after eliminating dominated options: the set of choices where getting more requires paying more.

functions.name: strictly_dominates
functions.formula: `a.cost <= b.cost && a.effect >= b.effect && (a.cost < b.cost || a.effect > b.effect)`
functions.example: for `sms_ai = Alternative::new("SMS + AI triage", 90_000.0, 3_500.0)` and `phone = Alternative::new("Phone calls", 120_000.0, 2_200.0)`, `strictly_dominates(&sms_ai, &phone) == true` and `strictly_dominates(&phone, &sms_ai) == false`

functions.name: efficiency_frontier
functions.example: for `options = [Alternative::new("Do nothing", 0.0, 0.0), Alternative::new("SMS reminders", 20_000.0, 2_000.0), Alternative::new("Phone calls", 120_000.0, 2_200.0), Alternative::new("SMS + AI triage", 90_000.0, 3_500.0)]`, `efficiency_frontier(&options)` yields names `["Do nothing", "SMS reminders", "SMS + AI triage"]` (Phone calls is strictly dominated)

functions.name: frontier_icers
functions.example: for the frontier `["Do nothing", "SMS reminders", "SMS + AI triage"]`, `frontier_icers(&frontier)` gives `[Some(10.0), Some(46.67...)]`

modules.name: qaly_shortfall_and_severity_modifiers
modules.title: QALY Shortfall and Severity Modifiers
modules.summary: QALY shortfall measures how much future health a disease takes from patients compared to the general population. NICE uses it to apply **severity modifiers**: the sicker the population, the more each QALY gained is worth — up to 1.7× the standard threshold.

functions.name: severity_weight
functions.formula: `1.7` if `absolute_shortfall >= 18.0 || proportional_shortfall >= 0.95`; else `1.2` if `absolute_shortfall >= 12.0 || proportional_shortfall >= 0.85`; else `1.0`. Whichever measure gives the higher weight applies.

modules.name: opportunity_cost
modules.title: Opportunity Cost
modules.summary: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when you commit a resource. In a health system with a fixed budget, spending £1 million on one thing means £1 million of health *not* produced somewhere else.

functions.name: opportunity_cost
functions.formula: the maximum of the supplied values (values may be in any consistent unit; negative values allowed).

modules.name: analysis_perspective
modules.title: Analysis Perspective
modules.summary: Perspective defines *whose* costs and benefits count in an economic analysis: the payer's, the provider's, or society's as a whole. The same intervention can look brilliant from one perspective and terrible from another, so every economic evaluation must declare its perspective up front — the perspective determines which line items exist.

functions.name: net_value_from_perspective
functions.formula: `sum over items where item.included_in(perspective) of item.amount`
functions.example: for the three-item worked-example inventory (payer savings +£420,000 counted for payer and societal; patient time +£300,000 counted for societal only; harm -£600,000 counted for societal only), `net_value_from_perspective(&items, Perspective::Payer) == 420_000.0` and `net_value_from_perspective(&items, Perspective::Societal) == 120_000.0`

functions.name: patient_time_value
functions.signature: patient_time_value(visits: f64, hours_per_visit: f64, value_per_hour: f64) -> f64

functions.name: false_reassurance_harm
functions.signature: false_reassurance_harm(visits: f64, false_reassurance_rate: f64, extra_treatment_cost_per_case: f64) -> f64

modules.name: time_horizon
modules.title: Time Horizon
modules.summary: The time horizon is the period over which an analysis counts costs and effects. It must be long enough to capture all meaningful differences between the options being compared.

functions.name: net_present_value
functions.formula: `Σ_t net_flows[t] / (1 + discount_rate)^t`, where `t` is the index into `net_flows` (year 0 first, undiscounted)

functions.name: net_benefit_at_horizon
functions.signature: net_benefit_at_horizon(implementation_cost: f64, annual_benefit: f64, annual_running_cost: f64, horizon_years: f64) -> f64

functions.name: break_even_horizon_years
functions.signature: break_even_horizon_years(implementation_cost: f64, annual_benefit: f64, annual_running_cost: f64) -> Option<f64>
functions.returns_none_when: `annual_benefit - annual_running_cost == 0.0` (the case never breaks even; a negative annual net benefit yields a negative, meaningless horizon rather than `None`)

functions.name: net_benefit_by_horizons
functions.signature: net_benefit_by_horizons(implementation_cost: f64, annual_benefit: f64, annual_running_cost: f64, horizons_years: &[f64]) -> Vec<(f64, f64)>
functions.formula: for each `h` in `horizons_years`, `(h, net_benefit_at_horizon(implementation_cost, annual_benefit, annual_running_cost, h))`, in the input order

modules.name: discounting_and_time_preference
modules.title: Discounting and Time Preference
modules.summary: Discounting converts future costs and benefits into present values, because a benefit today is worth more than the same benefit in five years.

functions.name: present_value
functions.signature: present_value(future_value: f64, rate: f64, years: f64) -> f64

functions.name: annuity_present_value
functions.signature: annuity_present_value(annual_benefit: f64, rate: f64, years: f64) -> f64
functions.formula: `annual_benefit * (1.0 - (1.0 + rate).powf(-years)) / rate`, except when `rate == 0.0`, which returns the r→0 limit `annual_benefit * years` instead (since the closed form is 0/0 at `rate = 0`)

functions.name: delayed_present_value
functions.signature: delayed_present_value(undelayed_pv: f64, rate: f64, delay_years: f64) -> f64

modules.name: marginal_vs_average_cost
modules.title: Marginal vs Average Cost
modules.summary: Average cost is total cost divided by units produced. Marginal cost is the cost of producing one *additional* (or one fewer) unit.

functions.name: marginal_saving
functions.formula: `ΔQ × MC` (units freed × marginal/variable cost per unit)

functions.name: crosses_capacity_step
functions.example: with `step = ward_bed_days_per_year(20.0)` (`7_300.0`), `crosses_capacity_step(7_300.0, step) == true` and `crosses_capacity_step(1_000.0, step) == false`

modules.name: value_of_a_statistical_life
modules.title: Value of a Statistical Life (VSL)
modules.summary: The value of a statistical life (VSL) — called the "value of a prevented fatality" (VPF) in UK usage — is the amount a *population* is collectively willing to pay to reduce the risk of one statistical death, derived from wage-risk trade-off studies (how much extra pay workers demand for riskier jobs) and stated-preference surveys. It is not the price of any identified individual's life; it is a population-risk construct used in regulatory cost-benefit analysis (transport safety, environmental regulation), and it comes from a different theoretical tradition than `willingness_to_pay_thresholds`' QALY × threshold valuation — labour-market revealed preference rather than health-budget-constrained methodology.

modules.name: cross_currency_icer_comparison
modules.title: Cross-Currency ICER Comparison
modules.summary: Comparing an [`crate::incremental_cost_effectiveness_ratio`] computed in one country's currency against another country's [`crate::willingness_to_pay_thresholds`] — or pooling cost data collected across a multinational trial — requires an explicit, auditable currency-conversion step. ISPOR's methods guidance for multinational trials recommends converting resource costs using purchasing power parity (PPP) — not market exchange rates — when comparing the real economic value of resources across countries, and reserves market FX rates for what they're actually for: modelling real cross-border cash payment flows.

functions.name: convert
functions.signature: convert(rate: &ExchangeRate<'static, iso::Currency>, amount: Money<'static, iso::Currency>) -> Result<Money<'static, iso::Currency>, MoneyError>
functions.formula: `rate.convert(&amount)` — converts `amount` into another currency using an explicit, auditable exchange rate (a PPP conversion factor for comparing real economic value across countries, or a market FX rate only for modelling actual cross-border cash payment flows).
functions.returns_none_when: Err: `amount`'s currency does not match `rate`'s `from` currency; returns `Err(MoneyError::Overflow)` iff the conversion arithmetic overflows.
functions.example: converting `Money::from_major(45_000, iso::USD)` with `ExchangeRate::new(iso::USD, iso::GBP, Decimal::new(72, 2))` gives `Ok(Money::from_major(32_400, iso::GBP))`

functions.name: adopt_at_threshold
functions.formula: `icer_in_threshold_currency.lt(threshold)` — `Ok(true)` (adopt) if the ICER is strictly less than the threshold, `Ok(false)` (reject) otherwise.
functions.returns_none_when: Err: `icer_in_threshold_currency` and `threshold` are in different currencies (by design: a caller that passes an unconverted ICER is caught, not silently miscompared).
functions.example: `adopt_at_threshold(&Money::from_major(32_400, iso::GBP), &Money::from_major(34_000, iso::GBP)) == Ok(true)`; the same ICER converted at a market rate instead of PPP gives `Money::from_major(35_550, iso::GBP)`, and `adopt_at_threshold` on that value against the same threshold gives `Ok(false)`

modules.name: multi_criteria_decision_analysis
modules.title: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA)
modules.summary: Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) is a weighted-sum scoring model used in health technology assessment when a single ICER/willingness-to-pay threshold doesn't capture everything a decision-maker cares about: equity, unmet need, innovation, budget impact, disease severity. Each criterion gets a weight reflecting its importance (elicited from stakeholders, weights summing to 1) and each option gets a normalized score per criterion (typically 0–1); the overall score is the weighted sum — the same mathematical shape as a software vendor-selection scorecard.

modules.name: carbon_footprint_per_qaly
modules.title: Carbon Footprint per QALY
modules.summary: Carbon per QALY is an efficiency ratio — an intervention's carbon emissions (or emissions avoided) divided by the QALYs it delivers — directly analogous to cost per QALY, letting an intervention's carbon efficiency be assessed alongside its cost efficiency. A "carbon-adjusted net monetary benefit" goes a step further, monetizing the carbon impact using the UK Green Book's official non-traded carbon values and netting it against the standard net monetary benefit.

functions.name: carbon_adjusted_net_monetary_benefit
functions.signature: carbon_adjusted_net_monetary_benefit(net_monetary_benefit: f64, emissions_tonnes_co2e: f64, carbon_value_per_tonne: f64) -> f64

modules.name: sensitivity_analysis
modules.title: Sensitivity Analysis
modules.summary: Deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) varies one assumption at a time across a plausible range to see whether the conclusion survives. The standard visualization is a tornado diagram: parameters ranked by how much they swing the result, dominant parameter on top.

functions.name: rank_by_swing
functions.example: given `[("license price", 48_000.0), ("time saved", 2_376_000.0), ("working days", 240_000.0), ("loaded cost", 880_000.0)]`, after `rank_by_swing`, `swings[0].0 == "time saved"` and `swings[3].0 == "license price"`

modules.name: probabilistic_sensitivity_analysis
modules.title: Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis (PSA)
modules.summary: PSA assigns a probability distribution to every uncertain parameter, samples them all simultaneously thousands of times (Monte Carlo), and reports the *probability* that an option is the best choice — instead of a single point estimate.

functions.name: net_monetary_benefit
functions.signature: net_monetary_benefit(threshold: f64, effect: f64, cost: f64) -> f64

functions.name: ceac
functions.formula: for each joint draw index `i`, finds the option with the highest NMB (ties go to the earliest-listed option) and tallies a win; returns `wins_j / n` per option (fractions sum to 1).
functions.returns_none_when: there are no options, no draws (the first option's slice has length 0), or the options' draw counts differ.

functions.name: probability_positive
functions.returns_none_when: `draws` is empty. Draws exactly equal to zero do not count as positive.

functions.name: percentile
functions.formula: sorts a copy of `draws` (via `f64::total_cmp`), then linearly interpolates between the order statistics bracketing rank `(p / 100).clamp(0, 1) × (len - 1)`.
functions.returns_none_when: `draws` is empty. `p` outside `[0, 100]` is clamped, not an error.

functions.name: simulate_migration_net_benefits
functions.signature: simulate_migration_net_benefits(case: &MigrationCase, n: usize, seed: u64) -> Option<Vec<f64>>
functions.formula: for each of `n` draws, samples `cost ~ Gamma(cost_mean, cost_sd)`, `annual ~ Normal(benefit_mean, benefit_sd)`, `duration ~ Uniform(duration_low, duration_high)`, and computes `duration × annual − cost` (discounting omitted).
functions.returns_none_when: `case.cost_mean` or `case.cost_sd` is not strictly positive (propagated from `Lcg::gamma_mean_sd`).
functions.example: for the worked-example `MigrationCase`, `simulate_migration_net_benefits(&case, 10_000, 42)` gives a mean net benefit within `30_000.0` of `775_000.0` and calling it twice with the same `case`, `n`, and `seed` produces identical `Vec<f64>` results (determinism).

modules.name: expected_value_of_perfect_information
modules.title: Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI)
modules.summary: EVPI is the maximum amount a decision-maker should pay to eliminate uncertainty before deciding — the formal price of "let's run a study first". It is the gap between deciding with perfect foresight (in each possible world you pick that world's best option) and deciding now (you must commit to the single option that is best on average).

functions.name: expected_nmb_of_best_option
functions.formula: `max_j Σ_i (scenarios[i].probability × scenarios[i].option_nmbs[j])` — expectation per option across worlds, then the max over options ("decide now").
functions.returns_none_when: `scenarios` is empty, the first scenario has no options, or any scenario's option list has a different length than the first (every scenario must offer the same options).
functions.example: `expected_nmb_of_best_option(&[Scenario { probability: 0.6, option_nmbs: vec![8.0, 0.0] }, Scenario { probability: 0.4, option_nmbs: vec![-3.0, 0.0] }]) == Some(3.6)`

functions.name: expected_nmb_with_perfect_information
functions.formula: `Σ_i (scenarios[i].probability × max_j scenarios[i].option_nmbs[j])` — max over options inside each world ("perfect foresight"), then the probability-weighted sum across worlds.
functions.returns_none_when: `scenarios` is empty or any scenario has an empty option list.

functions.name: evpi
functions.returns_none_when: either of the two calls above returns `None` (i.e. `scenarios` is empty or options are missing). Always ≥ 0; exactly 0 when the same option wins in every world.

functions.name: evpi_from_psa_draws
functions.formula: builds one `Scenario` per draw with equal probability `1 / draws.len()`, then computes `evpi` on those scenarios.
functions.returns_none_when: `draws` is empty (or, transitively through `evpi`, if a draw has no options).
functions.example: 6 draws of `[8.0, 0.0]` and 4 draws of `[-3.0, 0.0]` (reproducing the `p = 0.6/0.4` worlds) → `Some(1.2)`

modules.name: expected_value_of_sample_information
modules.title: Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI)
modules.summary: EVSI is the value of a *specific proposed study* — a given design, a given sample size — before it is run, as opposed to expected value of perfect information (EVPI), which prices eliminating all uncertainty outright. EVSI answers the question a research funder actually faces: "is *this* trial, at *this* size, worth its cost?"

functions.name: evsi_normal_approximation
functions.signature: evsi_normal_approximation(evpi: f64, sample_size: f64, prior_equivalent_sample_size: f64) -> Option<f64>
functions.formula: `evpi × sample_size / (sample_size + prior_equivalent_sample_size)` — the closed-form normal approximation, valid for a single uncertain parameter under a (roughly) conjugate normal-normal model.

modules.name: benefits_realization
modules.title: Benefits Realization
modules.summary: Benefits realization management (BRM) is the discipline of identifying, baselining, tracking, and *evidencing* that the benefits promised in a business case actually materialized after delivery. In UK public investment it lives inside HM Treasury's Green Book **Five Case Model**; in medicine, its cousin is post-market surveillance.

modules.name: real_options_valuation
modules.title: Real Options Valuation
modules.summary: Real options valuation applies financial option-pricing logic to real (non-financial-market) investment decisions — specifically here, the *option to expand* a project later if it succeeds, without being obligated to. A simplified one-period binomial model (Cox, Ross, Rubinstein, 1979) values this: the project's value either rises (`up_factor`) or falls (`down_factor`) by the next decision point; the option to expand is only exercised if it is profitable in that state (payoff floored at zero, since it is a genuine *option*, not an obligation); a risk-neutral probability weights the two states.

functions.name: risk_neutral_probability
functions.signature: risk_neutral_probability(risk_free_rate: f64, down_factor: f64, up_factor: f64) -> Option<f64>
functions.returns_none_when: `up_factor == down_factor` (the two binomial states are indistinguishable — a deliberate exact-equality guard on the degenerate input, not a rounding-sensitive comparison).

functions.name: option_to_expand_value
functions.signature: option_to_expand_value(project_value: f64, up_factor: f64, down_factor: f64, expansion_cost: f64, risk_free_rate: f64) -> Option<f64>
functions.formula: computes `p` via `risk_neutral_probability`, then `payoff_up = max(project_value * up_factor - expansion_cost, 0.0)`, `payoff_down = max(project_value * down_factor - expansion_cost, 0.0)`, then `(p * payoff_up + (1.0 - p) * payoff_down) / (1.0 + risk_free_rate)`.
functions.example: `option_to_expand_value(1_000_000.0, 1.5, 0.5, 600_000.0, 0.08) ≈ Some(483_333.333_333)` (522,000 / 1.08, a non-terminating decimal — verified by running the code, not hand-derived).

modules.name: bed_days_saved

"Bed days saved" — through earlier discharge, admission avoidance, or virtual wards — is the workhorse benefit of NHS digital business cases, and the most commonly overvalued: the *kind* of value depends entirely on what happens to the freed bed.

modules.summary: Length of stay is the number of days from hospital admission to discharge — the core flow-efficiency metric of inpatient care. UK acute means run around 4–5 days; every excess day consumes a scarce bed and exposes the patient to hospital-acquired risks.

Behind the prices sits a national unit-costing infrastructure: the **National Cost Collection (NCC)** and the **PSSRU Unit Costs of Health and Social Care** compendium (~80 standard unit costs: GP consultation, nurse-hour by band, ED attendance — the default source in UK economic evaluations).

modules.summary: PAF is the proportion of a disease or outcome's burden in a population that is attributable to a specific risk-factor exposure — the share that would disappear if the exposure were removed entirely. It converts "this risk factor doubles your odds" into a population-level number a commissioner can plan around: how many cases, and how much cost, a given exposure is really worth chasing.

modules.name: number_needed_to_screen

It is NNT's screening-programme-level analogue: NNT asks how many must be *treated* to prevent one outcome; NNS asks how many must go through the whole screen-and-then-treat pathway to get there.

modules.name: wearable_validation
modules.title: Wearable Validation
modules.summary: Validation metrics quantify how well a wearable's measurements agree with a clinical gold standard (ECG for heart rate, polysomnography for sleep): MAPE, Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), and Bland–Altman limits of agreement — plus the operational metrics that gate real-world data quality: wear-time compliance and data completeness.

functions.name: mape_percent
functions.returns_none_when: `measured` is empty, `measured.len() != reference.len()`, or any `reference` value is `0.0`

functions.name: concordance_correlation
functions.formula: `2 * s_xy / (s_x² + s_y² + (x̄ - ȳ)²)` using population (1/n) moments
functions.returns_none_when: `measured` is empty, `measured.len() != reference.len()`, or the denominator `s_x² + s_y² + (x̄ - ȳ)²` is `0.0` (both series constant with equal means)
functions.example: for `reference = [60.0, 70.0, 80.0, 90.0, 100.0]`, `concordance_correlation(&reference, &reference) == Some(1.0)`; with a constant +10 bias, `concordance_correlation(&biased, &reference) == Some(0.8)`

functions.name: bland_altman
functions.formula: `mean_bias = mean(measured_i - reference_i)`; `lower_limit = mean_bias - 1.96 * sd`; `upper_limit = mean_bias + 1.96 * sd`, where `sd` is the sample standard deviation (n − 1 denominator) of the paired differences
functions.returns_none_when: `measured.len() != reference.len()` or there are fewer than 2 pairs (`n < 2`, since the sample SD needs `n >= 2`)

modules.name: exact_cents_cost_allocation
modules.title: Exact-Cents Cost Allocation
modules.summary: Splitting a total amount of money — a shared grant, an infrastructure bill, a budget-impact total — across several recipients by naive percentage arithmetic routinely produces parts that don't sum back to the original total. This is the "Money" bug class from Martin Fowler's *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture* (2002): rounding each recipient's share independently loses (or gains) cents, and the error surfaces only when someone reconciles the parts against the whole.

functions.name: allocate_by_shares
functions.signature: allocate_by_shares(total: Money<'static, iso::Currency>, shares: &[u32]) -> Result<Vec<Money<'static, iso::Currency>>, MoneyError>
functions.formula: each recipient first receives `floor(total_minor_units × share / sum(shares))` minor units, then any leftover minor units are distributed one at a time to the recipients with the largest fractional remainder. Guarantee: `sum(parts) == total`, always, regardless of how unevenly `total` divides among `shares`.
functions.returns_none_when: Err: `rusty-money`'s internal allocation fails (for example, on arithmetic overflow). It does **not** return an error merely because `total` doesn't divide evenly among `shares` — that case is exactly what the largest remainder method handles correctly.
functions.example: `allocate_by_shares(Money::from_major(100, iso::USD), &[1, 1, 1])` returns 3 parts whose sum equals `Money::from_major(100, iso::USD)` exactly (even though $100.00 ÷ 3 does not divide evenly); which specific recipient receives the leftover cent is an internal tie-break detail of `Money::allocate`, not part of the contract.

modules.name: currency_safe_cost_rollup
modules.title: Currency-Safe Cost Rollup
modules.summary: Summing many money line items — monthly invoices, per-site costs, multi-year budget-impact figures — with ordinary binary floating-point (`f64`) numbers accumulates small representation errors, because most decimal fractions ($1,234.56, for instance) aren't exactly representable in binary floating point (Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic," 1991). Each individual error is tiny, but a model summing hundreds of line items over several years can drift by fractions of a cent — and the drift depends on the *order* the additions happen in, which makes it non-reproducible.

functions.name: sum_line_items
functions.formula: folds `items` with `Money::add`, exact regardless of item count or summation order.
functions.returns_none_when: Err: `items` is empty (there is no well-defined total, and no currency to report one in). Also propagates any `MoneyError` `add` returns while folding — notably `Err(MoneyError::CurrencyMismatch)` if the items aren't all in the same currency, or `Err(MoneyError::Overflow)` on arithmetic overflow.
functions.example: `sum_line_items(&vec![Money::from_minor(123_456, iso::USD); 12]).unwrap() == Money::from_minor(1_481_472, iso::USD)` (twelve $1,234.56 invoices sum to exactly $14,814.72)

functions.name: apply_multiplier
functions.signature: apply_multiplier(total: Money<'static, iso::Currency>, multiplier: Decimal) -> Result<Money<'static, iso::Currency>, MoneyError>
functions.formula: `total.mul(multiplier)` — an exact `Decimal` product that may carry more decimal places than the currency's minor-unit exponent; the caller must round explicitly afterward with a stated rounding rule.
functions.example: `apply_multiplier(Money::from_minor(1_481_472, iso::USD), Decimal::new(105, 2)).unwrap()` then `.round(2, Round::HalfEven) == Money::from_minor(1_555_546, iso::USD)` ($14,814.72 × 1.05 = exact $15,555.456, rounds half-even to $15,555.46)

functions.name: budget_variance
functions.signature: budget_variance(actual: Money<'static, iso::Currency>, budgeted: Money<'static, iso::Currency>) -> Result<Money<'static, iso::Currency>, MoneyError>
functions.formula: `actual.sub(budgeted)` — positive means over budget, negative means under budget, exact to the minor unit.
functions.returns_none_when: Err: `actual` and `budgeted` are in different currencies.
functions.example: `budget_variance(Money::from_minor(1_555_546, iso::USD), Money::from_minor(1_481_472, iso::USD)).unwrap() == Money::from_minor(74_074, iso::USD)` ($15,555.46 actual against a $14,814.72 budget is exactly $740.74 over)
